narrative:
The model estimated a 59% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, versus a 41% chance of passing. In this admissions process, that risk level was high enough to deny your application; it is a warning about bar-exam readiness, not a judgment that you cannot succeed.

Your application was denied mainly because three factors had the strongest influence. The most influential was your LSAT score: 22.50, well below the 37.18 average among accepted students, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. The second was your third-year decile: at 1.00, far from the accepted-student average of 5.79, it also pushed toward failure. The third was your family income bracket: being in the high bracket pushed toward passing, but this positive signal was weaker than the two academic concerns and could not offset them.

Next, ask admissions for feedback and whether an appeal or reconsideration is possible. If you reapply, focus on raising your LSAT through structured preparation, and provide evidence that your third-year academic performance does not reflect your current bar-exam readiness—such as improved coursework, structured legal study, or work/study experience. A higher LSAT and a credible plan to address the academic signal would most directly reduce the failure risk the model identified.
